title: Forget Everything (Statistical Mechanics Part 1)

contents.markdown:
**EDIT: I somehow missed that John Wentworth and David Lorell** ~**are also in the middle of a sequence**~ **have written one post on this same topic** [**here**](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/keGhMbnLNdTAHa4bv/generalized-stat-mech-the-boltzmann-approach)**.** ~**I will see where this goes from here!**~ **This sequence will continue!**

*Introduction to a sequence on the statistical thermodynamics of some things and maybe eventually everything. This will make more sense if you have a basic grasp on quantum mechanics, but if you're willing to accept "energy comes in discrete units" as a premise then you should be mostly fine.*

The title of this post has a double meaning:

1.  Forget the thermodynamics you've learnt before, because statistical mechanics starts from information theory.
2.  The main principle of doing things with statistical mechanics is can be summed up as follows:

**Forget as much as possible, then find a way to forget some more.**

Particle(s) in a Box
====================

All of practical thermodynamics (chemistry, engines, etc.) relies on the same procedure, although you will rarely see it written like this:

1.  Take systems which we know something about
2.  Allow them to interact in a controlled way
3.  Forget as much as possible
4.  If we have set our systems correctly, the information that is lost will allow us to learn some information somewhere else.

For example, consider a particle in a box.

![](https://39669.cdn.cke-cs.com/rQvD3VnunXZu34m86e5f/images/41c16300e3013cdf839838d28ae90f87ee8fd586f1f2bfac.png)

What does it mean to "forget everything"? One way is forgetting where the particle is, so our knowledge of the particle's position could be represented by a uniform distribution over the interior of the box.

Now imagine we connect this box to another box:

![](https://39669.cdn.cke-cs.com/rQvD3VnunXZu34m86e5f/images/24c5e72f82c78e8e7e6d24bebd7e5665ae3e8afc7629a71e.png)

If we forget everything about the particle now, we should also forget which box it is in!

If we instead have a lot of particles in our first box, we might describe it as a box full of gas. If we connect this to another box and forget where the particles are, we would expect to find half in the first box and half in the second box. This means we can explain why gases expand to fill space without reference to anything except information theory.

![](https://39669.cdn.cke-cs.com/rQvD3VnunXZu34m86e5f/images/693272e9ab7cfa3cd7a6ee9b1458ef61cc8df2f8837e51e3.png)

A new question might be, how much have we forgotten? Our knowledge gas particle has gone from the following distribution over boxes 1 and 2

\\(\mathrm P(\mathrm {Box}) = \cases{1 & Box 1 \ 0 & Box 2}\\)

To the distribution

\\(\mathrm P(\mathrm {Box}) = \cases{0.5 & Box 1 \\0.5 & Box 2}\\)

Which is the loss of 1 bit of information per particle. Now lets put that information to work.

The Piston
----------

Imagine a box with a movable partition. The partition restricts particles to one side of the box. If the partition moves to the right, then the particles can access a larger portion of the box:

![](https://39669.cdn.cke-cs.com/rQvD3VnunXZu34m86e5f/images/41ff338aa8fd1282a5ae5f3b75b5db56e5401e95a80cca96.png)

In this case, to forget as much as possible about the particles means to assume they are in the largest possible space, which involves the partition being all the way over to the right. Of course there is the matter of forgetting where the partition is, but we can safely ignore this as long as the number of particles is large enough.

What if we have a small number of particles on the right side of the partition?

![](https://39669.cdn.cke-cs.com/rQvD3VnunXZu34m86e5f/images/21951deae786dc5bc1f670a4d985f7c39e161332490937a3.png)

We might expect the partition to move some, but not all, of the way over, when we forget as much as possible. Since the region in which the pink particles can live has decreased, we have **gained knowledge about their position**. By coupling forgetting and learning, anything is possible. The question is, how much knowledge have we gained?

Maths of the Piston
-------------------

Let the walls of the box be at coordinates 0 and 1, and let \\(x\\) be the horizontal coordinate of the piston. The position of each green particle can be expressed as a uniform distribution over \\((0, x)\\), which has entropy \\(\log_2(x)\\), and likewise each pink particle's position is uniform over \\((x, 1)\\), giving entropy \\(\log_2(1-x)\\).

If we have \\(n_g\\) green particles and \\(n_p\\) pink particles, the total entropy becomes \\(n_g \log_2(x) + n_p \log_2(1-x)\\), which has a minimum at \\(x = \frac{n_g}{n_g + n_p}\\). This means that the total volume occupied by each population of particles is proportional to the number of particles.

If we wanted to ditch this information-based way of thinking about things, we could invent some construct which is proportional to \\(\frac{n_g}{x}\\) for the green particles and \\(\frac{n_p}{1-x}\\) for the pink particles, and demand they be equal. Since the region with the higher value of this construct presses harder on the partition, and pushes it away, we might call this construct "pressure".

If we start with \\(x = 1/3\\) and \\(n_g = 2 \times n_p\\), we will end up with \\(x = 2/3\\). We will have "forgotten" \\(n_g\\) bits of information and learned \\(n_p\\) bits of information. In total this is a net loss of \\(n_p\\) bits of information, which are lost to the void.

The task of building a good engine is the task of minimizing the amount of information we lose.

Conclusions
===========

We can, rather naturally and intuitively, reframe the behaviour of gases in a piston in terms of information first and pressure later. This will be a major theme of this sequence. Quantities like pressure and temperature naturally arise as a consequence of the ultimate rule of statistical mechanics:

**You can only forget, never remember.**

title: Measuring Learned Optimization in Small Transformer Models

contents.markdown:
*This is original, independent research carried out in March and April of 2024.*

![A graphical abstract: A formula generates data which is used to pretrain models. These are then subject to three RL tasks of varying difficulty. The reward function of a model can be identified by looking at a task-specific prediction of optimization as comapared to measured optimization. ](https://39669.cdn.cke-cs.com/rQvD3VnunXZu34m86e5f/images/66e64d42b1a3df9c4e9f6320320410fcd67b438ed27bafa5.png)

The degree to which a a policy optimizes the future can be quantified mathematically. A set of of very small transformer models were pretrained to predict the next token in a mathematical sequence, then subjected to reinforcement learning finetuning.

The optimizing power of each model can be predicted with high accuracy based on each model's score on its own RL task. By comparing predictions of optimization based on scores on each different RL task, a model's original reinforcement objective can be identified.

A related measure for impact can also be derived mathematically, and given a theoretical lower bound based on RL score. This gives further information about model behavior, and allows for the same analysis as the measure of optimization.

I also investigate the possibility of getting models to self-evaluate optimization and impact, with limited success.

Methods
=======

Pretraining on Sequence Prediction
----------------------------------

I defined a simple mathematical sequence defined by the following stochastic recurrence relation. This produces a pseudo-random but (to 98%) predictable sequence, alternating between elements of \\(\{0,...,7\}\\) on even values of \\(t\\) and \\(\{8,...,15\}\\) on odd values of \\(t\\).

\\(s_t = \big ( \cases{((\overset{16}{\underset{i=1}{\prod}}(s_{t-i}+1)\mod 17)\mod 8)  & with probability 98% \  \in\{0,...,7\} & with probabiltiy 2%} \big )  + 8 \times (t\mod2)\\)

I then trained a small encoder-only transformer model to predict the next element in the sequence given the previous 20 elements of the sequence.

This was followed by a reinforcement-learning phase in which the transformer was used to generate the next token on odd values of \\(n\\) only, and the recurrence relation was used to generate the value of \\(s_{t+1}\\). If \\(s_{t+1}\\) was in \\(\{0,2,4,6\}\\), this was used as a "successful" example to reinforce the model. I used a temperature of 1 when generating these sequences to introduce some randomness, but the temperature was reduced to 0 during evaluations and when calculating optimization.

A small amount of "maintenance" training (much lower learning rate) was used during this phase to ensure that model performance on the predictive tasks for even values of \\(t\\) was maintained. Without this I saw rapid loss of performance on the "maintenance" dataset. I also found that I was unable to include "unsuccessful" examples (i.e. where \\(s_{t+1} \notin \{0,2,4,6\}\\)) with even a tiny negative learning rate, as this caused worsened performance at all tasks. Here is a typical set of results from training and evaluation:

I carried out this training on \\(N=5\\) models per size for four model sizes between 18k and 402k parameters, giving the following plot:

![On the left is a plot showing pretraining and maintenance loss, on the right is a graph showing success rate on a task. Both are a function of parameters. Pretraining and maintenance loss show a U-shape, success generally increases with the number of parameters.](https://39669.cdn.cke-cs.com/rQvD3VnunXZu34m86e5f/images/9770dfb53023a4df3532db8ff7820124bbf9c86c95a0c251.png)

Pretraining loss increases over the last few model sizes, and the loss/time plots (some of which I have put in the Supplementary Information at the bottom of this post) showed signs of overfitting in the large models. Regularization was employed during training (0.01 weight decay in an AdamW optimizer, 10% dropout rate for neurons) so perhaps a larger dataset size is required to totally avoid this.

I then repeated the RL phase twice, once with \\(s_{t+1} \in \{0,4\}\\) being reinforced,  (\\(n_{good}\\) = 2) and once with \\(s_{t+1} \in \{0,1,2,4,5,6\}\\) being reinforced (\\(n_{good}\\) = 6). Here is a plot of success rate against model size across all three conditions.

![A plot showing success rate against model size on different tasks. Success rate is better than chance in all conditions, and increases with model size in all conditions.](https://39669.cdn.cke-cs.com/rQvD3VnunXZu34m86e5f/images/81cfc786c16024566a1f83de2f98d940103fb75ca2f2e8e4.png)

This plot shows mean \\(\pm\\) standard error. In all cases model performance is a lot better than chance, and increases with model size.

Measuring Optimization
----------------------

I used a Monte Carlo simulation to measure the nats of optimization that are being applied to \\(s_{t+1}\\) using the split-history method I've previously outlined. This involves taking the difference in entropy between two distributions:

![A diagram with the following equation at the top: Op(F, P; A) = H(F'|P'') - H(F). Below are two Bayes nets. The one on the left has nodes P, A,and F with nodes P to A, P to F and A to F. The network on the left has nodes P, P'', A', and F'. It has arrows P' to F', P'' to A', and A' to F'.](https://39669.cdn.cke-cs.com/rQvD3VnunXZu34m86e5f/images/2a190bce92510a6cf76f17a3da1be0adf232cf4609807524.png)

The algorithm in practice is this:

1.  Take a bunch of sequence examples from the testing data, ensuring that \\(t\\) is odd.
2.  Feed them into the models to get a value for \\(s_t\\), append to the sequence.
3.  Use the sequence-generator to get a set of values for \\(s_{t+1}\\)
4.  Look at the entropy of the resulting distribution over \\(s_{t+1}\\), this is the optimized entropy.
5.  For each sequence from the training data, and get a value of \\(s_t'\\) from this.
6.  Repeat Steps 3-4 with the entire data set as \\(...,s_{t-2},s_{t-1}\\) prepended to \\(s_t'\\), get one sample of "unoptimized" entropy
7.  Repeat Steps 5-6 with each sequence from the initial dataset, take the average unoptimized entropy
8.  Optimization = unoptimized entropy - optimized entropy

Here is a schematic illustration:

![A diagram showing the process outlined above. The final equation is Op(F, P; A) =  -H(F) + H(F'|P'')](https://39669.cdn.cke-cs.com/rQvD3VnunXZu34m86e5f/images/8e9b0cb324ec8657e00bbf7e96a849d51210e5668216a80d.png)

On the left, the model is able to respond to each sequence fed into it, so it can optimize the future creating a low-entropy distribution. On the right, the model is forced to give a fixed response to the external input, which is then appended to the sequences. This means that it cannot optimize the future and the entropy is higher.

I ran this calculation 10 times with 200 sequences in \\(P\\) and took an average to get an idea of the model's optimizing capability. I also tested the sequence-generating function's self-optimization.

![A plot showing optimization against model size under three conditions. The fewer potential results are "good", the higher the optimization for a given model size. Optimization increases with model size in all cases.](https://39669.cdn.cke-cs.com/rQvD3VnunXZu34m86e5f/images/b753ae9f718e9593157b0594a9827ae2fccda3e23a9c5c1d.png)

The fact that the sequence is optimizing itself mostly just amounts to saying that it is not a random walk, which we already knew. It is a good sanity check that all of the models get values either equal to or above this, and that optimization improves with model size.

Results
=======

Optimization vs RL Success Rate
-------------------------------

Optimization is calculated as the entropy difference of two distributions. Let us consider three parameters: \\(n\\): the number of possible outcomes; \\(p\\): the proportion of outcomes which are "successes"; and \\(s\\):  the chance that the model achieves a successful outcome.

Assuming the model is "ambivalent" over successful outcomes, and likewise ambivalent over failed outcomes, then the value of \\(\mathrm H(F)\\) should be equal to \\(-s \ln(\frac{s}{np}) -(1-s) \ln(\frac{1-s}{n(1-p)})\\). If we then assume that all outcomes are equally likely when the model's outputs are "randomized", then \\(\mathrm H(F' |P'')\\) is just \\(-\ln(\frac1n)\\). If we take the difference we get the following expression:

\\(\mathrm{Op} \approx s \ln(\frac s {np}) + (1-s) \ln(\frac{1-s}{n(1-p)}) - \ln(\frac1n)\\)

\\(\mathrm{Op} \approx s \ln\frac s p + s \ln\frac1n + (1-s)\ln\frac{1-s}{1-p} + \ln \frac1n - s \ln\frac1n - \ln\frac1n\\)

\\(\mathrm{Op} \approx s \ln \frac sp + (1-s) \ln \frac {1-s}{1-p}\\)

Now I can plot this theoretical value for \\(\mathrm{Op}\\) against \\(s\\) for \\(p \in \{0.25, 0.5, 0.75\}\\), and also plot all of the models on the same axes. Since we see a lot of run-to-run variation in model performance, I'll plot the raw data per model rather than statistics.

![A plot showing optimization plotted against success rate for three conditions. Three series of points are shown, each sitting on a similarly-colored curve.](https://39669.cdn.cke-cs.com/rQvD3VnunXZu34m86e5f/images/8011aade0d0309cf7bd742dcb4c27525f488cdca4fa390ef.png)

I tried to find some galaxy-brained variable change which would make those three curves the same, but I couldn't. Instead I will just plot the predicted value of \\(\mathrm{Op}\\) (based on their success rate) for each model against the actual value:

![The headline figure is repeated but with annotations. All the points lie very close to the theoretical line y=x.](https://39669.cdn.cke-cs.com/rQvD3VnunXZu34m86e5f/images/538357310086e320ccfc355ee445948d3761aaef7d9bf415.png)

In theory none of the models should fall below the dashed line representing the equation derived above. In practice they do. Some of this is error in measurements, but I'm sure some of it is also due to errors in my assumptions. In particular the assumption that \\(\mathrm H(F'|P'')\\) is completely flat is unlikely to hold.

On the other hand, there there is no reason at all why the models shouldn't fall quite far above the theoretical line. Consider the \\(n_{good}=6\\) case, so successful values are\\(s_{t+1} \in\{0,1,2,4,5,6\}\\). If the model ends up with a 85:15 ratio of values 2 and 3 for \\(s_{t+1}\\)(and never gets any other number, which is impossible in this specific case but that's not important for my point) then it will have a success rate of 0.85, which implies an \\(\mathrm{Op}\\) of 0.03, but its actual \\(\mathrm {Op}\\) will be 1.66!

![A plot showing potential different outcomes to training. These outcomes are listed below.](https://39669.cdn.cke-cs.com/rQvD3VnunXZu34m86e5f/images/5ff511265b29647adae65cf66d268420fb9cccb359a20441.png)

Sorry for the poor aesthetics of this diagram, it's very difficult to get the point across that the bottom left one has the lowest optimization.

For a given training performance (in this case I've tried to make them all ~75% correct) the model might do one of several things:

1.  Optimize for reinforced results and against non-reinforced results in an unbiased way
2.  Optimize against non-reinforced results correctly, but only optimize for some of the successful results
3.  Optimize for reinforced results correctly, but only optimize against some of the non-reinforced results
4.  Behave in such a way that certain reinforced results are optimized against and certain non-reinforced results are optimized for.

The last three are examples of one type of inner misalignment. All three are characterized by excess optimization compared to the "correct" answer.

Cross-Objective Evaluation
--------------------------

The fact that most of the models don't sit far above the line shows that the RL is doing its job! They are (mostly) pursuing the training objective faithfully, without picking up on other objectives. I simulate what might happen if a model picks up on an "incorrect" objective by cross-evaluating models on each others' tasks:

![A plot showing Measured Optimization against Score on n_good=4 task. The points corresponding to policies trained on the n_good=4 task lie on the theoretical curve, models trained on other tasks cluster to the left and above it.](https://39669.cdn.cke-cs.com/rQvD3VnunXZu34m86e5f/images/ddc7872b17137e6e7ae912087b3f4ee9851d6f08db2f00b8.png)

Now it becomes obvious that the \\(n_{good} = 4\\)-trained models are behaving correctly whereas the other models are not. This is important since a model trained on the \\(n_{good}=2\\) task will typically have a good score on the \\(n_{good}=4\\) task, sometimes even higher than a similarly-sized model trained on the \\(n_{good}=4\\) task (!) but this plot clearly shows us that something is going wrong.

It becomes even clearer if we instead take the value of \\(\mathrm{Op}\\) implied by the formula from above, and plot it against the actual value of \\(\mathrm{Op}\\). Here are the results for all three tasks:

![A plot with predicted optimization on the x axis and measured on the y axis. The purple points for n_good=2 sit on a purple y=x line. The other points mainly sit above the line.](https://39669.cdn.cke-cs.com/rQvD3VnunXZu34m86e5f/images/4c58e378aae8de1b6481e3a60b137af67f25db4fd37ddc65.png)

![As above but with blue n_good=4 points sitting on a blue line, and the other clusters above.](https://39669.cdn.cke-cs.com/rQvD3VnunXZu34m86e5f/images/19c6b810d21c47feb38161b89d9ddaee2d1179f3c9dac7e3.png)

![As above but with yellow n_good = 2 points on the line and other clusters above it.](https://39669.cdn.cke-cs.com/rQvD3VnunXZu34m86e5f/images/942299d9b0ffa1a1bf2728f0fe597d600f3de9f5cb996299.png)

By comparing implied and measured \\(\mathrm{Op}\\), we can separate the models trained on a given reward signal from ones trained on a different reward signal, even when one of the reward signals is a subset of the other.

Optimization vs Impact
----------------------

I will now take a second look at the measure for \\(\mathrm{Op}\\). What I really wanted all along is to measure a policy's **impact** on the world, and optimizing the future is only one way in which this can happen. Another way is flattening the possibilities out! Consider the following informal diagram. "Original" distribution is not well-defined here, the point is just to give an intuitive explanation:

![A spiky original distribution is subject to two types of impact. With Optimizing impact, the distribution becomes spikier, and lower entropy. With Flattening impact, the distribution becomes flatter and higher entropy.](https://39669.cdn.cke-cs.com/rQvD3VnunXZu34m86e5f/images/908952891d9fd8aabd53c65df571edd8c53d32b7414e6479.png)

The motivation and derivations for this can be found in Appendix A, with longer proofs listed in Appendix B, but the upshot is that we can define a new function: \\(\mathrm{Imp}(F, P;A)\\) using the KL divergence of \\(F\\) and \\(F'\\) like this:

![](https://39669.cdn.cke-cs.com/rQvD3VnunXZu34m86e5f/images/0a60047c8d65435fe6a2eea80538e6c0d42285786f2a6fec.png)

Which if we have a task success rate \\(s\\) in \\(F\\) and \\(s'\\) in \\(F'\\) must obey the following equation:

\\(\mathrm{Imp}(F,P;A) \equiv D_{KL}(F \Vert F'|P'') \ge s \ln \frac{s}{s'} + (1-s) \ln \frac{1-s}{1-s'} \equiv \mathrm{Imp}_{min}(F,P;A)\\)\\(\\)

This can be measured using the same split-history method used to measure \\(\mathrm{Op}\\):

![A plot showing impact against parameters. Impact increases with parameter count and decreases with n_good](https://39669.cdn.cke-cs.com/rQvD3VnunXZu34m86e5f/images/8243070003ca5cdd20c3ca1aafe22d053746ffc489e6b269.png)

The lower bound \\(\mathrm{Imp}_{min}\\) can be calculated from success rates and the two can be compared:

![A model showing Measured Impact plotted against Minimum Impact From Score. The points form a plume around y = 2.6x + 0.059](https://39669.cdn.cke-cs.com/rQvD3VnunXZu34m86e5f/images/efde29f6640d0c45076f7b37c35331456faf7fdf3e5ee0a4.png)

Larger models have a higher impact, but they also tend to have a lower ratio of \\(\mathrm{Imp} / \mathrm{Imp}_{min}\\)than do the smaller ones. The single-line fit is also somewhat misleading, and actually the models appear to lie on three separate lines. I note that the values of  \\(\mathrm{Imp}_{min}\\) are somewhat low in this case, rather than our measured impact being unexpectedly high. Our measure for \\(\mathrm{Imp}\\) may not be perfect in this case.

I think the difference between \\(\mathrm{Imp}\\) and \\(\mathrm{Imp}_{min}\\) tells us something. In this case it tells us that the success rates in \\(F'\\) are actually quite high:

![A plot showing success in F' against parameter count. Models for all values of n_good have better performance than chance, and it seems to slightly scale with model size.](https://39669.cdn.cke-cs.com/rQvD3VnunXZu34m86e5f/images/bb8187f1d13c92137aa43599f61f97e9494ab1168f7bbc62.png)

Success rate in \\(F'\\) doesn't scale very much at all with model size, which indicates that models of all sizes exhibit roughly the same bias in outputs, based on statistical regularities in the data (e.g. a "13" is more commonly followed by a "2" than a "15" is). It might also be an artefact stemming from an uneven distribution of numbers in our sequence by default.

This highlights an important point about split-history measures: they only pick up on the effects of "active" inference in the policy, not on biases in the outputs which are produced during training.  We don't have to use a split-history method to generate \\(F'\\), we can think up plenty of alternative ways to generate a comparison future, and therefore generate a family of measures for \\(\mathrm{Imp}\\) and \\(\mathrm{Op}\\):

*   Use a privileged "Do nothing" token as the model's output
*   Use a totally random output token
*   Use an untrained model, or a pretrained (but not finetuned) model

Despite these problems, if we repeat cross-objective evaluation using \\(\mathrm{Imp}\\) we get these plots:

![A plot showing measured Impact against Imp_min based on the n_good=2 task. Points trained on the "correct" task form a plume above the line y=x, whereas points trained on the n_good=4 task are squished over to the left.](https://39669.cdn.cke-cs.com/rQvD3VnunXZu34m86e5f/images/83abac6c9af2f8391de6fdcc8051747c04ad85a7786b8395.png)

The \\(n_{good} = 6\\) models don't appear because they do so badly on the task that \\(\mathrm{Imp}_{min}\\) cannot be calculated. 

![As above but the Imp_min is based on score on the n_good=4 task. The correct policies lie above the line y=x, the n_good=2 models lie far above them, and the n_good=6 lines are squished over to the left](https://39669.cdn.cke-cs.com/rQvD3VnunXZu34m86e5f/images/29ff70eb915d44886b0de5641b442369d9b1e0caeb1a89ae.png)

![](https://39669.cdn.cke-cs.com/rQvD3VnunXZu34m86e5f/images/103fab41e30dfa2196c3b12806c34f8bae57f94d9fbf23ce.png)

While the split is not as good as we saw with \\(\mathrm{Op}\\), it seems that models not trained on the "correct" fall along a line of lower gradient, and models trained on "incorrect" tasks have higher gradients i.e. the latter diverge from the \\(\mathrm{Imp}_{min}\\) line more rapidly.

There are many potential ways to visualize what's going on here, two more of which are in Appendix C at the end of this post.

Model Self-Evaluation
---------------------

A secondary goal of my work was to get models to evaluate their own optimizing power and impact. This is the reason for the maintenance training during finetuning. The self-evaluation scheme is the same as the optimization measuring scheme, except that instead of using the sequence-generating formula to get values for \\(s_{t+1}\\), I used the model's own predictive power to get expected distributions over \\(s_{t+1}\\) and \\(s_{t+1}'\\):

A plot showing measured optimization plotted against self-estimated optimzation. Models from the \\(n_{good}=6\\) task tend to fall on the line \\(y=x\\), but as \\(n_{good}\\) decreases, models fall further above the line.

![](https://39669.cdn.cke-cs.com/rQvD3VnunXZu34m86e5f/images/f31b93afd07149d53e451c89e19faa9e96347d2cd058f27c.png)

I suspect what's happened here is bog standard model bias. The more heavily the model is optimizing, the less even the distribution of examples of \\(s_{t+1}\\) it gets fed during the maintenance training. This might make it more biased towards predicting the rewarded variables after any sequence, which would cause it to underestimate \\(\mathrm{Op}\\).

The same can be done for \\(\mathrm{Imp}\\):

![](https://39669.cdn.cke-cs.com/rQvD3VnunXZu34m86e5f/images/81641dad85789c783d7ca580760c76c8df583c1c55ad2c00.png)

Which gives even worse results! I'm not sure whether or not this is also model bias. I don't have a tremendous amount of experience with ML, so I will not pursue this further in this post.

Conclusions
===========

The measure I've introduced for \\(\mathrm{Op}\\) seems to be predicted very well by theory, and might have utility in detecting how well a policy's results line up with an RL task when it can be predicted accurately. The measure for \\(\mathrm{Imp}\\) has some issues but shows some success towards the same goal. These can be considered complementary measures in many ways:

<table><tbody><tr><td style="text-align:center"><strong>Optimization</strong></td><td style="text-align:center"><strong>Impact</strong></td></tr><tr><td>Can be positive or negative, the sign gives us information</td><td>Always <span class="math-tex">\(\ge 0\)</span></td></tr><tr><td>Can be cancelled out by opposite-signed optimization elsewhere</td><td>Always a positive value, always at least adds up across different sources</td></tr><tr><td>No easy way to calculate theoretical values of Op in general (that I've found)</td><td><span class="math-tex">\(\mathrm{Imp}_{min}\)</span> can be calculated for any success/failure RL task</td></tr><tr><td>Excellent at identifying model behaviour in this case</td><td>Less good at identifying model behaviour in this case</td></tr></tbody></table>

I would be interested in applying both of these to more complex ML systems, but at the moment I don't any specific plans to do so, due to my very limited experience with ML. In Appendix A I also present equivalent measures which can be applied to the activations of a neural network.

A theoretical limitation of this work is that \\(\mathrm{Imp}_{min}\\) can only be calculated when a task is binary success/failure. If the policy is trying to maximize some function world-state then there's no simple formula for \\(\mathrm{Imp}_{min}\\) based on RL score. Work on these systems must either develop new maths or or find a way to break down utility maximization into a series of success/failure tasks, which can separately be evaluated for impact.

One practical limitation is in the self-evaluation stage. If the model's self-evaluation is biased, the measures of \\(\mathrm{Op}\\) and \\(\mathrm{Imp}\\) will be as well. This is especially problematic if \\(\mathrm{Op}\\) or \\(\mathrm{Imp}\\) is underestimated, allowing the policy to "lie" to us about how much optimization/impact it is doing. My wild guess is that AIs which include explicit world-modelling (such as DreamerV3) will be less biased by default, but that attempts at introducing impact regularization might reintroduce bias.

### Alex Turner's Existing Work

The expression for impact that I present here is totally independent with the AUP measure of impact as proposed by Alex Turner in [Towards a New Impact Measure](https://www.alignmentforum.org/posts/yEa7kwoMpsBgaBCgb/towards-a-new-impact-measure?_ga=2.10300598.204290679.1711976843-989286032.1698594240). There might be some subtle way in which they're related but I haven't thought about this enough to say more. I've also read [World State is the Wrong Abstraction for Impact](https://www.lesswrong.com/posts/pr3bLc2LtjARfK7nx/world-state-is-the-wrong-abstraction-for-impact) and agree with some of the points presented.

In response I would say that the metric I present here relies strongly on a model \\(F\\) of the future world state, so only details captured in \\(F\\) can affect the impact. In the limit where the future states only consist of \\(f \in \{\mathrm{success},\mathrm{failure}\}\\), then impact is trivially equal to the lower bound and excess impact = 0.

Appendices
==========

Appendix A: Impact and Differential Impact
------------------------------------------

### Derivation of \\(\mathrm{Imp}\\)

I present the motivation for, and derivation of, the measure of \\(\mathrm{Imp}\\) which I've used in this post. Returning to my estimator for \\(\mathrm{Op}\\):

\\(\mathrm{Op} \approx s \ln \frac s p + (1-s) \ln \frac{1-s}{1-p}\\)

If we think these being two distributions over \\(\{\mathrm{success},\mathrm{failure}\}\\) and think of \\(p\\) as the probability of succeeding by chance, this becomes the formula for a Kullback-Liebler divergence. For a quick recap, the KL divergence of two distributions over a variable \\(x \in \chi\\) follows this formula:

\\(D_{KL}(P \Vert Q) = \underset{x \in \chi}\sum P(x) \ln \frac{P(x)}{Q(x)}\\)

We could also estimate the probability of succeeding by chance using the split-history method. Let \\(s\\) be the success rate in \\(F\\), and \\(s'\\) be the success rate in \\(F'\\):

\\(s \ln \frac s {s'} + (1-s) \ln \frac{1-s}{1-s'}\\)

I will now present some results about KL divergences. I will start by defining \\(\chi_s \subset \chi\\) as the successful outcomes. Let us define a "baseline" probability distribution \\(P(x)\\) and from it a "baseline" success rate \\(s_0\\):

\\(s_0 = \underset{x_s \in \chi_s} \sum P(x_s)\\) 

Now imagine a policy acts on this distribution \\(P(x)\\) and changes it to a new distribution. If this policy has a success rate \\(s \in [s_0,1]\\), I define \\(Q(x)\\) as follows:

 \\(Q(x) = \cases{\frac s {s_0} P(x) & $x \in \chi_s$ \ \frac {1-s} {1-s_0} P(x) & $x \not\in \chi_s$}\\)

This is what we might expect to be the effects of a "minimum impact" policy: it makes successful outcomes more likely and unsuccesful outcomes less likely while leaving relative probabilities otherwise intact. The KL-divergence between \\(Q\\) and \\(P\\) can then be calculated, and it looks familiar:

\\(D_{KL} (Q \Vert P) = s \ln \frac{s}{s_0} + (1-s) \ln  \frac{1-s}{1-s_0}\\)

This is the minimum KL divergence possible in shifting a distribution to achieve a given success rate. If we change the variable names to \\(Q \to F, P \to F'|P'', s_0 \to s'\\) this allows us to write down the original relation for a policy's impact:

\\(\mathrm{Imp}(F,P;A) \equiv D_{KL}(F \Vert F'|P'') \ge s \ln \frac{s}{s'} + (1-s) \ln \frac{1-s}{1-s'} \equiv \mathrm{Imp}_{min}(F,P;A)\\)

### Differential Impact

In this case "differential" means "to do with differentiation". I've studied a construct I call differential optimization in the past, as it pertains to functions of real-valued variables. In this case if we have the functions \\(A = f(P)\\), \\(F = g(A, P) \equiv h(P)\\) we can define the following value:

\\(\mathrm{C}(F,P;A) = \frac{\partial F}{\partial P}|_{A \mathrm{varies}} / \frac{\partial F}{\partial P}|_{A \mathrm{constant}} \equiv \frac{\mathrm d h}{\mathrm d P} / \frac{\partial g}{\partial P}\\)

Intuitively, if \\(A\\) is "optimizing" \\(F\\), then when it is allowed to vary, \\(C \le 1\\) since \\(F\\) will change less when we allow \\(A\\) to change than when we fix \\(A\\). This led to the derivation of the differential optimization \\(\mathrm{Op} = -\ln (C)\\).

This can be extended to a differential impact metric:

 \\(\mathrm{Imp} \equiv - \ln(C) + C(C - 1)\\)

This has a minimum \\(\mathrm{Imp} = 0\\) at \\(C = 1\\), but it is speculative and has not been tested, so while I will present it here I can give no guarantees at all about its utility.

We can also extend this to vector-valued \\(\mathbf P, \mathbf F\\). If we define \\(\mathbf J_g\\) as the Jacobian when \\(A\\) varies, and \\(\mathbf J_h\\) as the Jacobian when \\(A\\) is constant, then \\(\mathbf C = \mathbf J_g^{-1} \mathbf J_h\\) we get the following values for \\(\mathrm{Op}\\) and \\(\mathrm{Imp}\\):

\\(\mathrm{Op} = -\ln|\mathbf C| \equiv \ln|\mathbf J_g|  - \ln|\mathbf J_h|\\)

\\(\mathrm {Imp} =-\ln|\mathbf C| + \mathrm{Tr}(\mathbf C \mathbf C^\mathrm T) - \mathrm{Tr}(\mathbf C)\\)

If \\(\mathbf P\\) and \\(\mathbf F\\) do not have the same dimension, then \\(\mathbf J_g^{-1}\\) does not exist and instead the following construction must be used:

\\(\mathrm{Op} = \frac12\ln|\mathbf J_g\mathbf J_g^\mathrm T| - \frac12\ln |\mathbf J_h \mathbf J_h^\mathrm T|\\)

\\(\mathrm {Imp} = \frac12\ln|\mathbf J_g\mathbf J_g^\mathrm T| - \frac12\ln |\mathbf J_h \mathbf J_h^\mathrm T| + \mathrm{Tr}(\mathbf J_h \mathbf J_h^\mathrm T(\mathbf J_g \mathbf J_g^\mathrm T)^{-1}) - \mathrm{Tr}(\mathbf J_g \mathbf J_h^T(\mathbf J_g \mathbf J_g^\mathrm T)^{-1})\\)

The motivation for constructions like this is to apply them to the activations of neural networks. For a network with width \\(w\\), and a backpropagation time of \\(t\\), I believe the time-complexity of this contains a polynomial term in \\(w\\) (possibly \\(\mathcal O(w^5(\log w)^2)\\) if using Bareiss algorithm) for the matrix inverse, and a term in \\(w \times t\\).

Appendix B: Proofs
------------------

### Derivation and proof of \\(\mathrm{Imp} \ge \mathrm{Imp}_{min}\\)

\\(D_{KL}(Q\Vert P) = \underset {x_s \in \chi_s} \sum\frac {s}{s_0}  P(x_s) \ln \frac {\frac {s}{s_0} P(x_s)}{P(x_s)} + \underset {x_u \not\in \chi_s} \sum \frac {1-s}{1-s_0} P(x_u) \ln \frac {\frac {1-s}{1-s_0} P(x_u)}{P(x_u)}\\)

\\(D_{KL}(Q \Vert P) = \frac{s}{s_0} \underset{x_s \in \chi_s} \sum P(x_s) \ln \frac{s}{s_0} + \frac{1-s}{1-s_0} \underset{x_u \not \in \chi_s} \sum P(x_u) \ln\frac{1-s}{1-s_0}\\)

\\(D_{KL}(Q \vert P) = \frac {s}{s_0} \times s_0 \ln\frac s {s_0} + \frac{1-s}{1-s_0}  \times (1-s_0) \ln \frac{1-s}{1-s_0}\\)

\\(D_{KL} (Q \Vert P) = s \ln \frac{s}{s_0} + (1-s) \ln  \frac{1-s}{1-s_0}\\)

I will prove that this choice of \\(Q\\) is a global minimum of \\(D_{KL}(Q \Vert P)\\) for a fixed \\(P\\).

Consider a distribution \\(R = Q + \delta Q\\), which involves moving some amount of probability mass \\(\delta\\) from \\(x_1\\) to \\(x_2\\). Without loss of generality, take both to be in \\(\chi_s\\) (they must both be in either \\(\chi_s\\) or \\(\chi_s^C\\) so that \\(R(x \in \chi_s) = s\\) holds) Consider the value of

\\(D_{KL}(R \Vert P) - D_{KL}(Q \Vert P)\\)

Trivially we only need to look at the components relevant to \\(x_1\\) and \\(x_2\\):

\\(R(x_1) \ln \frac {R(x_1)}{P(x_1)} + R(x_2) \ln \frac {R(x_2)}{P(x_2)} - Q(x_1) \ln \frac {Q(x_1)}{P(x_1)} - Q(x_2) \ln \frac {Q(x_2)}{P(x_2)}\\)

Expand values of \\(R(x)\\):

\\((Q(x_1)- \delta) \ln \frac{\frac{s}{s_0} P(x_1) - \delta}{P(x_1)} + (Q(x_2)+ \delta) \ln \frac{\frac{s}{s_0} P(x_2) + \delta}{P(x_2)} -Q(x_1)\ln \frac{\frac{s}{s_0} P(x_1)}{P(x_1)} - Q(x_2) \ln \frac{\frac{s}{s_0} P(x_2)}{P(x_2)}\\)

Expand and collect factors of \\(Q(x)\\), cancelling the \\(P(x)\\) on the bottom:

\\(Q(x_1) \ln \frac {\frac{s}{s_0} P(x_1) - \delta}{\frac{s}{s_0} P(x_1)} - \delta \ln \frac{\frac{s}{s_0} P(x_1) - \delta}{ P(x_1)} + Q(x_2) \ln \frac {\frac{s}{s_0} P(x_2) + \delta}{\frac{s}{s_0} P(x_2)} + \delta \ln \frac{\frac{s}{s_0} P(x_2) + \delta}{ P(x_2)}\\)

Collect the factors of \\(\delta\\), expand stuff to a \\(\ln(1 + y)\\) form:

\\(Q(x_1) \ln(1 - \frac{s_0}{s} \frac{\delta}{P(x_1)}) + Q(x_2) \ln(1 + \frac {s_0}{s} \frac{\delta}{P(x_2)}) + \delta \big [ \ln \frac{\frac{s}{s_0} P(x_2) + \delta}{ P(x_2)} - \ln \frac{\frac{s}{s_0} P(x_1) - \delta}{ P(x_1)}\big ]\\)

\\(Q(x_1) \ln(1 - \frac{s_0}{s} \frac{\delta}{P(x_1)}) + Q(x_2) \ln(1 + \frac {s_0}{s} \frac{\delta}{P(x_2)}) + \delta\big [\ln (1 + \frac {s_0}{s} \frac {\delta}{P(x_2)}) - \ln(1 - \frac {s_0}{s} \frac {\delta}{P(x_1)})\big ]\\)

Use the taylor expansion \\(\ln(1+y) \approx y - \frac12 y^2 ...\\) up to \\(\delta^2\\).

\\(Q(x_1)(-\frac{s_0}{s} \frac{\delta}{P(x_1)} - \frac12(-\frac{s_0}{s}\frac{\delta}{P(x_1)})^2...) + Q(x_2)(\frac{s_0}{s} \frac{\delta}{P(x_2)}-\frac12(\frac{s_0}{s}\frac{\delta}{P(x_2)})^2...) + \delta\big[(\frac{s_0}{s} \frac{\delta}{P(x_2)}...) - (\frac{s_0}{s} \frac{\delta}{P(x_1)}...)\big]\\)

Sub in \\(Q(x) = \frac s{s_0} P(x)\\), expand, cancel:

\\(-\frac 12\delta^2 \frac{s_0}{s}(\frac1{P(x_1)} + \frac1{P(x_2)}) + \delta^2\frac{s_0}{s}(\frac{1}{P(x_2)} + \frac{1}{P(x_1)})\\)

Subtract:

\\(\frac 12\delta^2 \frac{s_0}{s}(\frac1{P(x_1)} + \frac1{P(x_2)}) \ge 0\\)

Therefore \\(Q(x)\\) is a local minimum of \\(D_{KL}(Q\Vert P)\\) subject to our condition that \\(Q(X \in \chi_x) = s\\). \\(D_{KL}(Q \Vert P)\\) is convex in \\(Q\\) for fixed \\(P\\), therefore we have found the unique global minimum.

### Derivation of Differential Impact

The measure of \\(\mathrm{Op}\\) based on entropy that I've used here was based on the following comparison to differential optimization:

Consider the network \\(A = P\\), \\(F = P - (1-k) A\\). This gives \\(\mathrm{C}(F,P;A) = k\\) and \\(\mathrm{Op}(F,P;A) = -\ln k\\).

This can be extended to an entropic measure of \\(\mathrm{Op}\\) by considering uncertainty over \\(P\\), specifically:

 \\(P \sim N(\mu_P, \sigma_P)\\)

\\(A \sim N(\mu_P, \sigma_P)\\)

\\(F \sim N(k\mu_P, k \sigma_P)\\)

Using split-histories we get:

\\(P', P'' \sim N(\mu_P, \sigma_P)\\)

\\(A' \sim N(\mu_P, \sigma_P)\\)

\\(F'|P''=p'' \sim N(\mu_P-(1-k)p'', \sigma_P)\\)

If we take \\(\mathrm{Op}(F,P;A ) =H(F'|P'')-H(F)\\) this gives the familiar value of \\(\ln k\\). We may instead investigate the value of \\(\mathrm{Imp}(F,P;A) = D_{KL}(F\Vert F'|P'')\\). Letting \\(F\sim N(\mu_1, \sigma_1)\\), \\(F'|P'' \sim N(\mu_2, \sigma_2)\\) for brevity:

\\(\mathrm{Imp} = \ln(\frac{\sigma_2}{\sigma_1}) + \frac12 \frac{\sigma_1^2 + (\mu_1, \mu_2)^2}{\sigma_2^2} - \frac12\\)

Substituting:

\\(\mu_1 - \mu_2 = k \mu_P - \mu_P + (1-k)p'' = (1-k)p'' - (1-k)\mu_P\\)

\\((\mu_1-\mu_2)^2 = (1-k)^2(\mu_P^2 - 2\mu_Pp'' + p''^2)\\)

Taking \\(\mathbb E((\mu_1-\mu_2)^2)\\) with respect to \\(p''\\) requires taking \\(\mathbb E(p'') = \mu_P\\), \\(\mathbb E(p''^2) = \mu_P^2 + \sigma_P^2\\):

\\((\mu_1 - \mu_2)^2 = (1-k)^2(\mu_P^2 - 2\mu_P^2 +\mu_P^2 + \sigma_P^2) = \sigma_P^2\\)

\\(\sigma_1 = k\sigma_P\\)

\\(\sigma_2 = \sigma_P\\)

Substituting into our original equation:

\\(\mathrm {Imp} = \ln(1/k) + \frac12[k^2 + (1-k)^2\frac{\sigma_P^2}{\sigma_P^2}] - \frac12\\)

\\(\mathrm{Imp} = - \ln(k) + \frac12[k^2 + 1 - 2k + k^2] - \frac12\\)

\\(\mathrm{Imp} = -\ln(k) + k^2 - k\\)

\\(\mathrm{Imp} = - \ln(k) + k(k-1)\\)

Which, if we extend to \\(\mathrm{C}\\), gives

\\(\mathrm{Imp} = -\ln(C) +C(C- 1)\\)

### Derivation of Multivariate Differential Impact and Optimization

Let us take vectors \\(\mathbf p, \mathbf a, \mathbf f\\), and \\(\mathbf p', \mathbf p'', \mathbf a', \mathbf f'\\) in the same manner as above. Assume around some value of \\(\mathbf p\\) we have the following Jacobians.

\\(\mathbf J_f = \frac{\mathrm d \mathbf a}{\mathrm d \mathbf p}\\) \\(\mathbf J_g = \frac{\partial\mathbf f}{\partial\mathbf p}\\)  \\(\mathbf J_h = \frac{\mathrm d\mathbf f}{\mathrm d\mathbf p}\\)

Without loss of generality, take the means of all of these variables to be \\(\mathbf 0\\). There exists a formula for transforming a multivariate normal distribution[^3hb64deu3cw].

\\(\mathbf P \sim N(\mathbf 0, \mathbf \Sigma_\mathbf p)\\)

\\(\mathbf A \sim N(\mathbf 0, \mathbf J_f\mathbf\Sigma_\mathbf p\mathbf J_f^\mathrm T)\\)

\\(\mathbf F \sim N(\mathbf 0, \mathbf J_h \mathbf \Sigma_\mathbf p \mathbf J^\mathrm T_h)\\)

Now for \\(\mathbf f'|\mathbf p''\\), the mean will no longer be zero:

\\(\mathbf F'|\mathbf P''=\mathbf p'' \sim N((\mathbf J_h - \mathbf J_g) \mathbf p'', \mathbf J_g \mathbf \Sigma_\mathbf p \mathbf J_g^\mathrm T)\\)

We can calculate the KL divergence of \\(D_{KL}(\mathbf F\Vert \mathbf F'\vert \mathbf P'')\\) using another formula[^chms10yvueh]: 

\\(\frac12\big[\ln\frac{|\mathbf \Sigma_2|}{|\mathbf \Sigma_1|} - n_{dim} + \mathrm {Tr}(\mathbf \Sigma_2^{-1} \mathbf\Sigma_1) + (\mathbf \mu_2 -\mu_1)^{\mathrm T} \mathbf \Sigma_2^{-1}(\mu_2-\mu_1)]\\)

\\(\mathbf \Sigma_1 = \mathbf J_h \mathbf \Sigma_\mathbf p \mathbf J_h^\mathrm T\\)  
\\(\mathbf \Sigma_2 = \mathbf J_g \mathbf \Sigma_\mathbf p \mathbf J^\mathrm T_g\\)  
\\(\mu_2 - \mu_1 = (\mathbf J_h - \mathbf J_g ) \mathbf p''\\)

Therefore our impact will be:

\\(\frac12\Big [\ln\frac{|\mathbf J_g \mathbf \Sigma_\mathbf p\mathbf J_g^\mathrm T|}{|\mathbf J_h \mathbf \Sigma_\mathbf p\mathbf J_h^\mathrm T|} - n_{dim} + \mathrm Tr((\mathbf J_g \mathbf \Sigma_\mathbf p\mathbf J_g^\mathrm T)^{-1}\mathbf J_h \mathbf \Sigma_\mathbf p\mathbf J_h^\mathrm T) + \mathbf p''^\mathrm T (\mathbf J_h - \mathbf J_g)^\mathrm T(\mathbf J_g \mathbf \Sigma_\mathbf p\mathbf J_g^\mathrm T)^{-1}(\mathbf J_h - \mathbf J_g) \mathbf p''\Big]\\)

Taking the expected value of the third component is actually easy if you have access to the internet. We can see that it is of the form \\(\mathbb E(\mathbf v^\mathrm T \mathbf M \mathbf v)\\) where \\(\mathbf v\\) is multivariate normal. This has a closed-form solution[^ya6tgc8mdr8]:

\\(\mu^\mathrm T \mathbf M \mu + \mathrm{Tr}(\mathbf M \mathbf \Sigma)\\)

Therefore we have the following expression:

\\(\frac12\Big [\ln\frac{|\mathbf J_g \mathbf \Sigma_\mathbf p\mathbf J_g^\mathrm T|}{|\mathbf J_h \mathbf \Sigma_\mathbf p\mathbf J_h^\mathrm T|} - n_{dim} + \mathrm Tr((\mathbf J_g \mathbf \Sigma_\mathbf p\mathbf J_g^\mathrm T)^{-1}\mathbf J_h \mathbf \Sigma_\mathbf p\mathbf J_h^\mathrm T) + \mathrm{Tr}\Big((\mathbf J_h - \mathbf J_g)^\mathrm T(\mathbf J_g \mathbf \Sigma_\mathbf p\mathbf J_g^\mathrm T)^{-1}(\mathbf J_h - \mathbf J_g)\mathbf \Sigma_\mathbf p \Big)\Big]\\)

We can make some progress towards simplifying this if we take \\(\mathbf \Sigma_\mathbf p = \sigma_p \mathbb I\\), which in this case lets us cancel everything out involving a \\(\mathbf \Sigma _\mathbf p\\), since the scalar value of \\(\sigma_p\\) commutes with all matrices, \\(|\sigma_p\mathbb I| = \sigma_p^{n_{dim}}\\), and \\((\sigma_p \mathbb I)^{-1} = \sigma_p^{-1} \mathbb I\\). We will also assume that all the Jacobians are invertible.

\\(\frac12\Big [\ln\frac{|\mathbf J_g\mathbf J_g^\mathrm T|}{|\mathbf J_h \mathbf J_h^\mathrm T|} - n_{dim} +\mathrm Tr((\mathbf J_g \mathbf J_g^\mathrm T)^{-1}\mathbf J_h \mathbf J_h^\mathrm T) + \mathrm{Tr}\Big((\mathbf J_h - \mathbf J_g)^\mathrm T(\mathbf J_g \mathbf J_g^\mathrm T)^{-1}(\mathbf J_h - \mathbf J_g)\Big)\Big]\\)

\\(\frac12\Big [\ln\frac{|\mathbf J_g\mathbf J_g^\mathrm T|}{|\mathbf J_h \mathbf J_h^\mathrm T|} - n_{dim} + \mathrm Tr((\mathbf J_g\mathbf J_g^\mathrm T)^{-1}\mathbf J_h\mathbf J_h^\mathrm T) + \mathrm {Tr}(\mathbf J_h^\mathrm T (\mathbf J_g^{\mathrm T})^{-1}\mathbf J_g^{-1} \mathbf J_h) - \mathrm {Tr}(\mathbf J_h^\mathrm T (\mathbf J_g^{\mathrm T})^{-1}\mathbf J_g^{-1} \mathbf J_g) - \mathrm {Tr}(\mathbf J_g^\mathrm T (\mathbf J_g^{\mathrm T})^{-1}\mathbf J_g^{-1} \mathbf J_h) + \mathrm {Tr}(\mathbf J_g^\mathrm T (\mathbf J_g^{\mathrm T})^{-1}\mathbf J_g^{-1} \mathbf J_g) \Big]\\)

\\(\frac12\Big [\ln\frac{|\mathbf J_g\mathbf J_g^\mathrm T|}{|\mathbf J_h \mathbf J_h^\mathrm T|} - n_{dim} + \mathrm Tr((\mathbf J_g\mathbf J_g^\mathrm T)^{-1}\mathbf J_h\mathbf J_h^\mathrm T) + \mathrm {Tr}(\mathbf J_h^\mathrm T (\mathbf J_g\mathbf J_g^\mathrm T)^{-1} \mathbf J_h) - \mathrm {Tr}(\mathbf J_h^\mathrm T (\mathbf J_g^{\mathrm T})^{-1}) - \mathrm {Tr}(\mathbf J_g^{-1} \mathbf J_h) + \mathrm {Tr}(\mathbb I) \Big]\\)

\\(\frac12\Big [\ln\frac{|\mathbf J_g\mathbf J_g^\mathrm T|}{|\mathbf J_h \mathbf J_h^\mathrm T|} + \mathrm Tr((\mathbf J_g\mathbf J_g^\mathrm T)^{-1}\mathbf J_h\mathbf J_h^\mathrm T) + \mathrm {Tr}(\mathbf J_h^\mathrm T (\mathbf J_g \mathbf J_g^\mathrm T)^{-1} \mathbf J_h) - \mathrm {Tr}(\mathbf J_h^\mathrm T (\mathbf J_g^{\mathrm T})^{-1}) - \mathrm {Tr}(\mathbf J_g^{-1} \mathbf J_h)\Big]\\)

\\(\frac12\Big [\ln\frac{|\mathbf J_g\mathbf J_g^\mathrm T|}{|\mathbf J_h \mathbf J_h^\mathrm T|} + \mathrm Tr((\mathbf J_g\mathbf J_g^\mathrm T)^{-1}\mathbf J_h\mathbf J_h^\mathrm T) + \mathrm {Tr}(\mathbf J_h^\mathrm T (\mathbf J_g \mathbf J_g^\mathrm T)^{-1} \mathbf J_h) - 2 \mathrm {Tr}(\mathbf J_g^{-1} \mathbf J_h)\Big]\\)

Using the cyclic property of the trace:

\\(\frac12\Big [\ln\frac{|\mathbf J_g\mathbf J_g^\mathrm T|}{|\mathbf J_h \mathbf J_h^\mathrm T|} + 2 \mathrm Tr((\mathbf J_g\mathbf J_g^\mathrm T)^{-1}\mathbf J_h\mathbf J_h^\mathrm T) - 2 \mathrm {Tr}(\mathbf J_g^{-1} \mathbf J_h)\Big]\\)

\\(\frac12 \ln\frac{|\mathbf J_g \mathbf J_g^\mathrm T|}{|\mathbf J_h \mathbf J_h^\mathrm T|} + \mathrm Tr((\mathbf J_g^\mathrm T)^{-1}\mathbf J_g^{-1}\mathbf J_h \mathbf J_h^\mathrm T) - \mathrm {Tr}(\mathbf J_g^{-1} \mathbf J_h)\\)

\\(\frac12 \ln\frac{|\mathbf J_g \mathbf J_g^\mathrm T|}{|\mathbf J_h \mathbf J_h^\mathrm T|} + \mathrm Tr(\mathbf J_g^{-1}\mathbf J_h \mathbf J_h^\mathrm T(\mathbf J_g^\mathrm T)^{-1}) + \mathrm {Tr}(\mathbf J_g^{-1} \mathbf J_h)\\)

\\(\frac12 \ln|\mathbf J_g \mathbf J_g^\mathrm T(\mathbf J_h \mathbf J_h^\mathrm T)^{-1}| + \mathrm{Tr}(\mathbf J_g^{-1}\mathbf J_h (\mathbf J_g^{-1}\mathbf J_h)^\mathrm T) - \mathrm {Tr}(\mathbf J_g^{-1} \mathbf J_h)\\)

And if we define \\(\mathbf C = \mathbf J_g^{-1} \mathbf J_h\\) we get:

\\(-\ln|\mathbf C| + \mathrm{Tr}(\mathbf C \mathbf C^\mathrm T) - \mathrm{Tr}(\mathbf C)\\)

This seems to have the form of \\(-\ln(C^2) + C^2 - C\\), and in fact if we consider \\(\mathbf P\\), \\(\mathbf A\\), and \\(\mathbf F\\) to just be concatenations of variables, which maeans all the \\(\mathbf J\\) matrices are diagonal, we see that our equation has the form.

\\(- \ln (\prod C) + \sum C^2 - \sum C = \sum \big (- \ln C + C^2 - C \big)\\)

Which is a nice sanity check. The value of \\(\mathrm {Op}\\) is just the entropy difference \\(\frac 12 \ln \mathbf \Sigma_2 - \frac12 \ln \mathbf \Sigma_1\\) which simplifies to \\(- \ln|\mathbf C|\\) for free.

If the Jacobians are not invertible, but we assume that \\(\mathbf{J}_g \mathbf J_g^\mathrm T\\) is invertible, we instead get:

\\(\mathrm {Imp} = \frac12\ln|\mathbf J_g\mathbf J_g^\mathrm T| - \frac12\ln |\mathbf J_h \mathbf J_h^\mathrm T| + \mathrm{Tr}(\mathbf J_h \mathbf J_h^\mathrm T(\mathbf J_g \mathbf J_g^\mathrm T)^{-1}) - \mathrm{Tr}(\mathbf J_g \mathbf J_h^T(\mathbf J_g \mathbf J_g^\mathrm T)^{-1})\\)

Appendix C: Supplementary Plots
-------------------------------

### Other Ways to Visualize Impact Plots

Here I plotted the "Impact ratio" \\(\mathrm{Imp} / \mathrm{Imp}_{min}\\) against \\(\mathrm{Imp}_{min}\\):

![The next six plots are just re-visualizations of previously plotted and discussed data, so I'm not going to write a bespoke description for each one.](https://39669.cdn.cke-cs.com/rQvD3VnunXZu34m86e5f/images/6b209d23e14dc6d658100c209e31ad537204c23e0736ddd2.png)

![](https://39669.cdn.cke-cs.com/rQvD3VnunXZu34m86e5f/images/e7b1438d8dbfe46668bd8d2b3fa20d8fb10e12ef6e4e7ac6.png)

![](https://39669.cdn.cke-cs.com/rQvD3VnunXZu34m86e5f/images/bdb98026069f2f0431dedf52d08dd38065aeafda0390c05c.png)

Here I plotted "Excess Impact" \\(\mathrm{Imp} - \mathrm{Imp}_{min}\\) against \\(\mathrm{Imp}\\):

![](https://39669.cdn.cke-cs.com/rQvD3VnunXZu34m86e5f/images/d496aa398f262ad670bef3219c198ad5ebc2bb80fc71bb6e.png)

![](https://39669.cdn.cke-cs.com/rQvD3VnunXZu34m86e5f/images/e2fc717a663d0572a6ea04a659a7920e22bb1d6671e2b444.png)

![](https://39669.cdn.cke-cs.com/rQvD3VnunXZu34m86e5f/images/b0a9974cd043d95921007d19015d8560d01ccb7ffb364d80.png)

### Example training runs from \\(n_{good}\\) = 4

![There's 16 plots here, but none are important to the key point. Screen reader users I'm afraid you'll have to get someone else to nitpick the raw data.](https://39669.cdn.cke-cs.com/rQvD3VnunXZu34m86e5f/images/1d8403b705fe68e2dac014b0d5b981e96dd63c3b1b709e99.png)

This is original, independent research carried out in March and April of 2024.

The degree to which a a policy optimizes the future can be quantified mathematically. A set of of very small transformer models were pretrained to predict the next token in a mathematical sequence, then subjected to reinforcement learning finetuning.

The optimizing power of each model can be predicted with high accuracy based on each model's score on its own RL task. By comparing predictions of optimization based on scores on each different RL task, a model's original reinforcement objective can be identified.

A related measure for impact can also be derived mathematically, and given a theoretical lower bound based on RL score. This gives further information about model behavior, and allows for the same analysis as the measure of optimization.

I also investigate the possibility of getting models to self-evaluate optimization and impact, with limited success.


Methods


Pretraining on Sequence Prediction
I defined a simple mathematical sequence defined by the following stochastic recurrence relation. This produces a pseudo-random but (to 98%) predictable sequence, alternating between elements of {0,...,7} on even values of t and {8,...,15} on odd values of t.

st=(⎧⎪⎨⎪⎩((16∏i=1(st−i+1)mod17)mod8)  with probability 98% ∈{0,...,7} with probabiltiy 2%)+8×(tmod2)

I then trained a small encoder-only transformer model to predict the next element in the sequence given the previous 20 elements of the sequence.

This was followed by a reinforcement-learning phase in which the transformer was used to generate the next token on odd values of n only, and the recurrence relation was used to generate the value of st+1. If st+1 was in {0,2,4,6}, this was used as a "successful" example to reinforce the model. I used a temperature of 1 when generating these sequences to introduce some randomness, but the temperature was reduced to 0 during evaluations and when calculating optimization.

title: Briefly Extending Differential Optimization to Distributions

contents.markdown:
I've done some work on a definition of optimization which applies to "trajectories" in deterministic, differentiable models. What happens when we try and introduce uncertainty?

Suppose we have the following system consisting of three variables, the past \\(P\\), future \\(F\\), and some agent \\(A\\). The agent "acts" on the system to push the value of \\(F\\) 80% of the way towards being zero. We can think of this as follows: \\(A = 0.8P, F = P - A\\). Under these circumstances, \\(\frac{\partial F}{\partial P} |_{A \mathrm{varies}} / \frac{\partial P}{\partial F}|_{A \mathrm{constant}} = 0.2\\) which means our optimization function gives: \\(\mathrm{Op}(P, F; A) = - \log (|0.2|) \approx -1.61 \mathrm{nats}\\).

What if we instead consider a normal distribution over \\(P\\)? This must be parameterized by a mean \\(\mu_P\\) and a standard deviation \\(\sigma_P\\). Our formulae now look like this: 

\\(P \sim \mathcal N(\mu_P,\sigma_P)\\)  
\\(A \sim \mathcal N(0.8 \mu_P, 0.8 \sigma_P)\\)  
\\(F \sim \mathcal N(0.2 \mu_P, 0.2 \sigma_P)\\)

So what does it look like for \\(A\\) to "not depend" on \\(P\\)? We could just "pick" some value for \\(A\\) but this seems like cheating. What if we set up a new model, in which \\(F'\\) depends on \\(P'\\) and \\(A'\\), but \\(A'\\) depends on \\(P''\\) instead of \\(P'\\)? We can allow \\(P'\\) and \\(P''\\) to have the same distributions as before:

\\(P' \sim \mathcal N(\mu_P, \sigma_P)\\)  
\\(P'' \sim \mathcal N(\mu_P, \sigma_P)\\)  
\\(A \sim \mathcal N(0.8 \mu_P, 0.8 \mu_P)\\)

Calculating \\(F\\) is a bit more difficult. We can think of it as adding two **uncorrelated** normal distributions together. For normal distributions this just means adding the means and variances together. Our distributions have means \\(\mu_P\\) and \\(-0.8\mu_P\\), and variances \\(\sigma_P^2\\) and \\(0.64\sigma_P^2\\). Therefore we get a new distribution with mean \\(0.2 \mu_P\\) and variance \\(1.64 \sigma^2_P\\). This gives a standard deviation of \\(1.28\sigma_P\\).

\\(F' \sim \mathcal N(0.2 \mu_P,1.28 \sigma_P)\\)

What's the entropy of a normal distribution? Well, it's difficult to say properly, since entropy is poorly-defined on continuous variables. If one take the **limiting density of discrete points** one gets \\(\log(N) + \frac12 \log(2 \pi e\sigma^2)\\), where \\(N\\) goes to infinity. This is a problem unless we happen to be subtracting one entropy from another. So let's do that.

\\(\mathrm H(F) - \mathrm H(F') = \log(N) + \frac12\log(2\pi e \sigma_F^2)  - \log(N) - \frac12\log(2\pi e \sigma_{F'}^2)\\)  
\\(\mathrm H(F) - \mathrm H(F') = \frac12 \log(\sigma_F^2) - \frac12 \log(\sigma_{F'}^2)\\)  
\\(\mathrm H(F) - \mathrm H(F') = \log(\sigma_F) - \log(\sigma_{F'})\\)  
\\(\mathrm H(F) - \mathrm H(F') = \log(0.2\sigma_P) - \log(1.28\sigma_P)\\)  
\\(\mathrm H(F) - \mathrm H(F') = \log(0.2/1.28) \approx -1.86 \mathrm{nats}\\)

Ok so we got the sign wrong the first time. Nevermind. But there is another issue, this is higher than our previous value. This is because we're double-counting the variance from \\(P\\). We get the variance from \\(P'\\) and \\(P''\\) in \\(F'\\). We can correct this by changing the object of study from \\(\mathrm H(F')\\) to \\(\mathrm H(F'|P'')\\). This works exactly like you'd expect: it gives a weighted average of the value of \\(\mathrm H(F'|P'' = p'')\\) for all possible values of \\(p''\\). In this case it is trivial: for any fixed value of \\(p''\\) we get \\(F' \sim \mathcal N(\mu_P-0.8 p'', \sigma_P^2)\\). So lets take a look:

\\(\mathrm H(F'|P'') - \mathrm H(F) = \frac12 \log(\sigma_{F'|P''}^2) - \frac12 \log(\sigma_F^2)\\)  
\\(\mathrm H(F'|P'') - \mathrm H(F) = \log(\sigma_{F'|P''}) - \log(\sigma_F)\\)  
\\(\mathrm H(F'|P'') - \mathrm H(F) = \log(\sigma_F) - \frac12 \log(0.2\sigma_F)\\)  
\\(\mathrm H(F'|P'') - \mathrm H(F) = - \frac12 \log(0.2/1) \approx 1.61 \mathrm{nats}\\)

In any Bayes-ish net-ish model, if we can get an agent's behaviour in the following form:

![A network with nodes P, A, and F. There are arrows from P to F, P to A, and A to F](https://39669.cdn.cke-cs.com/rQvD3VnunXZu34m86e5f/images/06cd2edca1e63b9caa8afcba4ac487b45d2689d34904ecf3.png)

We can make the following transformation, and get \\(\mathrm{Op}(F,P;A) = \mathrm{H}(F'|P'') - H(F)\\).

![The network from above is shown. An arrow points from it to a new network with nodes P', P'', F'. and A'. There are arrows P' to F', P'' to A'', and A' to F'](https://39669.cdn.cke-cs.com/rQvD3VnunXZu34m86e5f/images/50b4342294e2983eec6a89605d5bf6e5be681a9beaa8961e.png)

I will think more about whether this extension is properly valid. One limitation is that we cannot have multiple sets of arrows into and out of \\(A\\), since this would mess with the splitting of \\(P\\).

I've done some work on a definition of optimization which applies to "trajectories" in deterministic, differentiable models. What happens when we try and introduce uncertainty?

Suppose we have the following system consisting of three variables, the past P, future F, and some agent A. The agent "acts" on the system to push the value of F 80% of the way towards being zero. We can think of this as follows: A=0.8P, F=P−A. Under these circumstances, ∂F∂P|A varies/∂P∂F|A constant=0.2 which means our optimization function gives: Op(P,F;A)=−log(|0.2|)≈−1.61 nats.

What if we instead consider a normal distribution over P? This must be parameterized by a mean μP and a standard deviation σP. Our formulae now look like this: 

P∼N(μP,σP)
A∼N(0.8μP,0.8σP)
F∼N(0.2μP,0.2σP)

So what does it look like for A to "not depend" on P? We could just "pick" some value for A but this seems like cheating. What if we set up a new model, in which F′ depends on P′ and A′, but A′ depends on P′′ instead of P′? We can allow P′ and P′′ to have the same distributions as before:

P′∼N(μP,σP)
P′′∼N(μP,σP)
A∼N(0.8μP,0.8μP)

Calculating F is a bit more difficult. We can think of it as adding two uncorrelated normal distributions together. For normal distributions this just means adding the means and variances together. Our distributions have means μP and −0.8μP, and variances σ2P and 0.64σ2P. Therefore we get a new distribution with mean 0.2μP and variance 1.64σ2P. This gives a standard deviation of 1.28σP.

F′∼N(0.2μP,1.28σP)

What's the entropy of a normal distribution? Well, it's difficult to say properly, since entropy is poorly-defined on continuous variables. If one take the limiting density of discrete points one gets log(N)+12log(2πeσ2), where N goes to infinity. This is a problem unless we happen to be subtracting one entropy from another. So let's do that.

H(F)−H(F′)=log(N)+12log(2πeσ2F)−log(N)−12log(2πeσ2F′)
H(F)−H(F′)=12log(σ2F)−12log(σ2F′)
H(F)−H(F′)=log(σF)−log(σF′)
H(F)−H(F′)=log(0.2σP)

title: Finite Factored Sets to Bayes Nets Part 2

contents.markdown:
This post assumes knowledge of category theory, finite factored sets, and Bayes nets.

The Setup
---------

I've already talked about DAGs and factor overlap Venn diagrams in a previous post, where I studied them within a category-theoretic framework. Here I'll also perform an explicit construction of them using set theory.

### DAGs

I have already discussed the set of directed acyclic graphs over \\(n\\) elements. We will denote the set of all DAGs of \\(n\\) elements as \\(\mathrm{DAG}(n)\\). Each Bayes net can be thought of as a set of pairs of elements \\(\{(i\in \{1,...,n\}, j \ne i \in \{1,...,n\}),...\}\\). 

This set can be converted into the category of Bayes nets over \\(n\\) elements by the addition of morphisms corresponding to "bookkeeping"-type relationships, which we will denote\\(\mathcal{DAG}_n\\). From this category, we can form a category whose elements are sets of the elements of \\(\mathcal{DAG}_n\\), subject to the following condition on a set \\(S\\):

(I'll slightly go against standard notation by using calligraphic acronyms for my category names i.e. \\(\mathcal{DAG}_n\\). I don't feel like any of my categories are definitely natural or useful enough to earn a "proper" bold name like \\(\mathbf{DAG}_n\\))

\\(\forall s \in S, b \in \mathrm{DAG}(n),~s\rightarrow b\implies b \in S\\)

This means that, if we can reach a given Bayes net \\(b\\) from any element \\(s\\) of our set \\(S\\), that Bayes net \\(b\\) must also be in \\(S\\). I refer to these as compatible sets and denote the category \\(\mathcal{CSB}_n\\) (standing for compatible sets of Bayes nets) as the category whose elements are compatible sets of \\(n\\) elements and for any two elements. To write it out fully:

\\(\mathrm{Ob}(\mathcal{CSB}_n) = \{S \in \mathbb{P}(\mathrm{DAG}(n)) \big | \forall s \in S, d \in \mathrm{DAG}(n), \mathcal{DAG}_n(s,d) = \{\rightarrow\} \implies d \in S\}\\)

\\(\mathcal{CSB}_n(A, B) = \cases{\{\rightarrow\} & $A \supseteq B$ \ \{\} & $A \subset B$}\\)

This should be read as "There is a unique morphism from \\(A\\) to \\(B\\) if and only if \\(A\\) is a weak superset of \\(B\\), otherwise there is no morphism". Orderings of this form always follow the rules required to create a category.

(Aside: sometimes we think about equivalence classes of Bayes nets. If we choose, we can first convert our Bayes nets to equivalence classes, then convert them to compatible sets, but this is not needed here)

This category has an initial object \\(\mathrm{Dis}_n\\) which is a set consisting of the discrete Bayes net (with no arrows at all) and therefore all Bayes nets. Less trivially it has a terminal object \\(\mathrm{Ind}_n\\) which contains exactly the Bayes nets which have an arrow between every pair of objects.

### Venn diagrams

Presence/absence Venn diagrams of \\(n\\) elements can be thought of as elements of the power-set of the power-set of the set \\(\{1,...,n\}\\). We can write this as \\(\mathbb{P}(\mathbb{P}(\{1,...,n\}))\\), but I will abbreviate this by writing \\(\mathbb {PP}(n)\\) in future. As before, we can form a category by ordering the sets, but in this case we will reverse the order of the morphisms, to create the category \\(\mathcal{FV}_n\\) (standing for factor Venn diagrams).

\\(\mathrm{Ob}(\mathcal{FV}_n) = \mathbb {PP}(n)\\)

\\(\mathcal{FV}_n(A,B) = \cases{\{\rightarrow\} & $A \subseteq B$ \ \{\} & $A \supset B$}\\)

This category has an initial object \\(\{\}\\) and a terminal object \\(\mathbb P({1,...,n})\\). 

Our categories look (something) like this:

![](https://39669.cdn.cke-cs.com/rQvD3VnunXZu34m86e5f/images/0294584a14ea461f14a31d203646e557d609ecfb6297a0be.png)

The Payoff
----------

### Functors \\(F_n\\) and \\(G_n\\)

There exist functors \\(\mathcal{FV}_n \overset{F_n}{\underset{G_n}{\rightleftarrows}} \mathcal{CSB}_n\\) which are naturally-defined with respect to the properties of joint probability distributions. There exist subcategories \\(\mathcal{FV}_n'\\) and \\(\mathcal{CSB}'_n\\) on which the functors \\(F_n\\) and \\(G_n\\) are totally inverse. The resulting category structure - I hope - will be useful for causal inference.

We will define compatibility \\(\mathrm{Cmp}(a,b)\\) between a set of elements \\(a \subseteq \{1,...,n\}\\)  and a Bayes net \\(b \in \mathrm{DAG}(n)\\) as follows: there must exist some node \\(a_i \in (a \hookrightarrow b)\\) (the hook arrow \\(\hookrightarrow\\) denotes the "inclusion" of the elements of \\(a\\) into \\(b\\), so it refers to the nodes in \\(b\\)which are elements of \\(a\\)) such that all other nodes \\(a_{\overline{i}} \in (a \hookrightarrow b)\\) are reachable via paths including only elements of \\(a \hookrightarrow b\\). 

\\(F_n:\mathcal{FV}_n \rightarrow \mathcal{CSB}_n\\) maps an object  \\(V \in \mathrm{Ob}(\mathcal{FV}_n)\\) is mapped to an object \\(S \in \mathrm{Ob}(\mathcal{CSB}_n)\\)according to the following rule: a Bayes net \\(s \in \mathrm{DAG}(n)\\) is present in \\(S\\) if and only if  \\(\mathrm{Cmp}(v,s)\\) holds for every set \\(v \in V\\).

We will quickly verify that this respects morphisms. Any \\(W\\) such that \\(V \rightarrow W\\) must contain at least all of the sets present in \\(V\\) (since \\(V \rightarrow W \iff V \subseteq W\\)) and possibly more. Therefore, any \\(r \in R = F_n(W)\\) must also follow all of the constraints imposed by \\(F_n(V)\\) and possibly \\(\\)more, so \\(S \supseteq R \iff S \rightarrow R\\).

Next, we wish to define \\(G_n\\). This requires a little finesse but isn't too difficult. We shall say that \\(G_n : \mathcal{CSB}_n \rightarrow \mathcal{FV}_n\\) maps an object \\(S \in \mathrm{Ob}(\mathcal{CSB}_n)\\) to an object \\(V \in \mathrm{Ob}(\mathcal{FV}_n)\\) according to the following rule: a set \\(v\\) is present in \\(V\\) if and only if \\(\mathrm{Cmp}(v,s)\\) holds for every Bayes net net \\(s \in S\\).

You may notice that this is almost the reverse of \\(F_n\\). This is by design. It's worth pausing for a moment to consider how they differ: \\(F_n\\) maps a factor overlap Venn diagram, constructed as a set of sets of items from \\(\{1,...,n\}\\), to a set of DAGs. We can think of it as starting with the complete set of DAGs, then going through our venn diagram \\(V\\), and for each \\(v \in V\\) throwing out the DAGs which don't conform. 

Conversely \\(G_n\\) maps a set of DAGs to a set of factor overlaps. We can think of it as starting with the completely full factor overlap Venn diagram, and for each DAG \\(s \in S\\), it throws out the factors which don't apply.

### Quick Examples

Our functors are not quite inverses: for an example consider the Venn diagram corresponding to the set \\(\{\{\},\{1\},\{2\},\{1,2\},\{1,3\},\{2,3\}\}\\) in \\(\mathcal{FV}_3\\). This is mapped by \\(F_3\\) to exactly the set of totally connected DAGs, which is the terminal object in \\(\mathcal{CSB}_3\\). The terminal object in \\(\mathcal{CSB}_3\\) is mapped by \\(G_3\\) to the terminal object \\(\{\{\},\{1\},\{2\},\{3\},\{1,2\},\{1,3\},\{2,3\},\{1,2,3\}\}\\) in \\(\mathcal{FV}_3\\). This corresponds to what I called "agnosticism" in our set of Venn diagrams in the last post.

Note that all objects \\(V \in \mathrm{Ob}(\mathcal{FV}_n)\\) such that \\(V = G_n(S \in \mathrm{Ob}(\mathcal{CSB}_n))\\) will contain the elements \\(\{\}\\) and \\(\{1\},...,\{n\}\\). We will often write this as a \\(...,\\) at the start of our set to save time.

For an example in the opposite direction, consider the set in \\(\mathcal{CSB}_3\\) which consists of the DAGs \\(\{(1,2),(3,2)\}\\), \\(\{(2,3),(1,3)\}\\) and the minimal set of other DAGs needed for this to be a valid element of \\(\mathcal{CSB}_3\\). This is mapped by \\(G_3\\) to the set \\(\{...,\{2,3\}\}\\), which is correspondingly mapped by \\(F_3\\) to the set of DAGs "downstream" of \\(\{(2,3)\}\\) and \\(\{(3,2)\}\\). I left sets like this out of our category in the previous post.

As an example where our functors are inverse to one another, consider the initial object of \\(\mathcal{FV}_3\\), which is the empty set \\(\{\}\\). This is mapped by \\(F_3\\) to the initial object of \\(\mathcal{CSB}_3\\), which is the set containing all elements of \\(\mathrm{DAG}(3)\\). This is compatible with no shared factors (as any shared factors impose constraints on Bayes nets) so is mapped by \\(G_3\\) right back to the empty set. This is true for any \\(n\\). It also applies to the terminal objects of any \\(\mathcal{FV}_n\\) and \\(\mathcal{CSB}_n\\) i.e. the total power set \\(\mathbb P(n)\\) and the set containing only fully-connected Bayes nets.

### Composing \\(F\\) and \\(G\\)

I am going to be lazy here and omit the subscript \\(n\\)s, just imagine I've put them in while I'm talking about general properties of all \\(F_n\\) and \\(G_n\\). Consider the following sequence starting with an element \\(V \in \mathrm{Ob}(\mathcal{FV})\\):

\\(V \overset F \rightarrow  S \overset G \rightarrow W \overset F \rightarrow R\\)

We have that \\(\forall v \in V, s \in S, \mathrm{Cmp}(v,s)\\). But \\(W\\) is defined as the set of all elements \\(w\\) (in the relevant set \\(\mathbb P(\{1,...,n\})\\) for our given \\(n\\)) such that \\(\forall s \in S, \mathrm{Cmp}(w,s)\\). This means that all of our elements of \\(V\\) are also elements of \\(W\\), in other words \\(V \subseteq W\\), and by the definition of our functor \\(F\\), \\(V \subseteq W \implies S \supseteq R\\).

But consider that we can reverse the logic: \\(\forall s \in S, w \in W,\mathrm{Cmp}(w,s)\\), but \\(R\\) is defined by \\(R = \{r \big | \forall w \in W, \mathrm{Cmp}(w,r)\}\\). This means that \\(S \subseteq R\\), which alongside \\(S \supseteq R\\) gives us \\(S = R\\).

This means that for all \\(V \in \mathrm{Ob}(\mathcal{FV})\\), \\(FGF(V) = F(V)\\). We can skip writing \\(V\\) and write this as \\(FGF = F\\), which is also the same as saying that \\(FG = I\\) (the identity morphism) on the image of \\(\mathcal{FV}\\) under \\(F\\). Conversely \\(GF = I\\) on the image of \\(\mathcal{CSB}\\) under \\(G\\).

This also means that \\((GF)^n = GF \forall n \in \mathbb N_+\\) so \\(GF\\) is a "projection" operator. It "projects" the elements of \\(\mathcal{FV}\\) onto a subcategory of \\(\mathcal{FV}\\), but then doesn't do anything further to elements that are already there. Likewise for \\(FG\\). \\(\\)

On our earlier diagram this all looks like this:

![](https://39669.cdn.cke-cs.com/rQvD3VnunXZu34m86e5f/images/73c28d55396e9b262303907b636efd98347cabcbf5f21d65.png)

\\(F\\) maps elements of \\(\mathcal{FV}\\) to a elements of \\(\mathcal{CSB}\\). We can label all of the elements that get "hit" as the image of \\(F\\), written \\(\mathrm{Im}(F)\\). Likewise \\(G\\) maps elements of \\(\mathcal{CSB}\\) to elements of \\(\mathcal{FV}\\), giving its image \\(\mathrm{Im}(G)\\). More importantly, \\(\mathrm{Im}(G) \equiv \mathrm{Im}(F)\\), with \\(F = G^{-1}\\) on these subcategories.

Properties of the Resulting Subcategories
-----------------------------------------

In category theory, we tend not to care about what the elements of a category *are*, only about the structure present in the morphisms. Therefore, rather than consider the rather clunky concept of two equivalent subcategories which are formed as the images of functors, we really just want to look at the resulting structure. Since I have no idea what to call it, I will call these categories \\(\mathcal{D}_n\\) for now. Since it makes no sense to perform inference on zero variables, we'll impose the limit \\(n > 0\\).

\\(\mathcal D_1 \equiv \mathbf{1}\\), which is the trivial category, with one element and one morphism. \\(\mathcal{D}_2\\) is a two element category with a morphism from one of its elements to the other. \\(\mathcal D_3\\) is a fifteen-element category with the structure discussed in the previous post.

\\(\mathcal D_4\\) has 1218 elements. This is the highest I've been able to enumerate using inefficient python code and a mediocre PC. I could perhaps try to get something to work on \\(\mathcal{D}_5\\), but no amount of efficiency can fight \\(O(2^{2^n})\\) for long. OEIS has nothing for the sequence 1,2,15,1218 so I'm stumped for better representations.

Combining Nodes in Bayes Nets
-----------------------------

One bookkeeping rule we have not used yet is the node-combining rule. This lets us map an object of \\(\mathcal{DAG}_n\\) to an object of \\(\mathcal{DAG}_{n-1}\\). We do this by combining two numbers \\(i \ne j \in \{1,...,n\}\\), replacing every \\(j\\) in an edge with \\(i\\), and then relabelling our numbers to be \\(\{1,...,n-1\}\\). We can also do the same for \\(\mathcal{FV}_n\\), mapping its elements to \\(\mathcal{FV}_{n-1}\\). This also works by combining two numbers as above.

For a given set \\(X\\) of possible "worlds", we might want to split it up into various partitions \\(X_i\\) (unlike in FFS, we do not impose any restrictions on these partitions). So if we have \\(X \in \{a,b,c,d\}\\) then the partition \\(X_1 \in \{a, b\lor c \lor d\}\\) is a totally valid variable, as is \\(X_2\{a \lor b, c \lor d\}\\). These "naturally" give a new variable \\((X_1, X_2) = \{a,b,c \lor d\}\\) when combined.

So, given a copy of \\(\mathcal{DAG}_n\\), we can "join" two variables together to map each element to an element of a copy of \\(\mathcal{DAG}_{n-1}\\). We can do this in \\(^nC_2\\) different ways. Up to now, we haven't really cared about what each node of a Bayes net actually was, but if we want to combine nodes we'll need to think about this. 

For a given set, \\(X\\) and a set of set of partitions \\(X_i\\), we can define \\(\mathcal{DAG}_{\{X_i\}}\\) as the category of Bayes nets over those partitions. We can then "glue together" all categories like this, to create \\(\mathcal{DAG}_X\\) for a set \\(X\\). We can likewise associate factor overlap diagrams with these, and create \\(\mathcal{FV}_{\{X_i\}}\\) for each set of disjoint partitions. By gluing together the relevant functors \\(F\\) and \\(G\\) for each pair of categories, we can make an enormous category \\(\mathcal{D}_X\\) corresponding to all sets of Bayes nets that a probability distribution over \\(\mathcal{D}_X\\) could obey.

Three Further Thoughts
----------------------

### Thought 1

What are the properties of the sets in \\(GF(\mathcal{FV})\\), i.e. the ones post-projection? Given a set of \\(m\\) factor overlaps (which includes \\(\{\},\{1\},...,\{n\}\\)), can we determine in some reasonable time (polynomial in \\(m\\) and \\(n\\) perhaps?) whether it is changed by \\(GF\\)? We have no good closed-form representation of the elements of \\(\mathcal D\\) yet.

### Thought 2

Bayes nets let us combine nodes (i.e. partitions) to get a new node and shrink the Bayes net, but is there some way to think about "blending" nodes continuously to move between Bayes nets with the same number of nodes?

So if we have our world \\(X \in \{a, b, c, d\}\\), then we can split this into two nodes in a two-element Bayes net: \\(X_1 \in \{a \lor b, c \lor d\}, X_2 \in \{ a \lor c, b \lor d \}\\). Or we could split it into two nodes like this: \\(X_1 \in \{a \lor b, c \lor d\}, X_3 \in \{a \lor d, b \lor c\}\\). Is there a way to embed these into a continuous space? Can we rotate between them? Can we describe probability distributions as elements of some space like \\(\mathbf P(\mathbb C^n)\\) or something, then Bayes nets as regions in this space?

### Thought 3

\\(\mathcal D_X\\) is unfathomably large even for small sets: we can have up to \\(\mathrm{Bell(n)}\\) different partitions (and \\(\mathrm{Bell}(n)\\) grows exponentially fast), so we may have up to \\(2^{\mathrm{Bell}(n)}\\) different Bayes nets, with the largest being
